_help: Add a term by copying any entry. difficulty: 1 Easy, 2 Medium, 3 Hard, 4 Expert. 'rush' is optional (answer = index of the correct choice). Terms must be letters only.

terms.clue: Longest and strongest bone in the body
terms.definition: The thigh bone, running from the hip to the knee.
terms.explanation: Its head sits in the acetabulum of the pelvis. Fractures of the femoral neck are common after falls in older people.

terms.clue: Largest artery, leaving the left ventricle
terms.definition: The main artery carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
terms.explanation: It ascends, arches and descends through the thorax and abdomen before dividing into the common iliac arteries at about L4.

rush.question: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, with different blood pressures in each arm. Suspect?
rush.why: Tearing pain to the back plus an arm-to-arm BP difference is classic for aortic dissection, a surgical emergency.

terms.clue: Dome-shaped muscle that drives breathing
terms.definition: The muscular sheet separating the chest from the abdomen; the main muscle of inspiration.
terms.explanation: Supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5 keeps the diaphragm alive). Contracting flattens the dome and draws air into the lungs.

rush.question: A spinal cord injury at C4 most threatens which function?
rush.why: The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, so high cervical injuries can paralyse the diaphragm.

terms.clue: Muscular tube from the pharynx to the stomach
terms.definition: The tube that carries swallowed food from the pharynx to the stomach.
terms.explanation: About 25 cm long. The lower esophageal sphincter normally stops stomach acid refluxing upward.

terms.clue: Hindbrain region coordinating balance and fine movement
terms.definition: The part of the brain behind the brainstem that coordinates movement, balance and posture.
terms.explanation: Latin for 'little brain'. Damage causes ataxia, intention tremor and difficulty with rapid alternating movements on the same side.

terms.clue: Seahorse-shaped structure for forming new memories
terms.definition: A structure in the medial temporal lobe essential for forming new memories.
terms.explanation: Named from the Greek for seahorse. It is one of the first regions affected in Alzheimer disease.

terms.clue: The socket of the hip joint
terms.definition: The cup-shaped cavity of the pelvis that receives the head of the femur.
terms.explanation: Formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis. The name means 'vinegar cup' in Latin.

terms.clue: Neck muscle named after its three attachments
terms.definition: A neck muscle running from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process of the skull.
terms.explanation: One side turns the head to the opposite side. It is supplied by the accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI).

terms.clue: Junction where one neuron signals to another
terms.definition: The junction across which a nerve impulse passes from one neuron to another cell.
terms.explanation: At chemical synapses, neurotransmitters cross the synaptic cleft and bind receptors on the next cell.

terms.clue: Functional unit of the kidney
terms.definition: The basic filtering and reabsorbing unit of the kidney.
terms.explanation: Each kidney has around a million nephrons, each made of a glomerulus and a tubule.

terms.clue: Water crossing a membrane toward more solute
terms.definition: Movement of water across a semipermeable membrane toward the side with higher solute concentration.
terms.explanation: This is why giving the wrong IV fluid can make cells swell or shrink.

terms.clue: Keeping the internal environment stable
terms.definition: Maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external change.
terms.explanation: Mostly achieved by negative feedback, such as sweating when body temperature rises.

terms.clue: Wave-like contractions that move food along the gut
terms.definition: Coordinated waves of smooth muscle contraction that push contents through the digestive tract.
terms.explanation: Controlled largely by the enteric nervous system. Absent bowel sounds can mean peristalsis has stopped (ileus).

terms.clue: Keeps alveoli from collapsing
terms.definition: A lipoprotein mixture that lowers surface tension in the alveoli.
terms.explanation: Made by type II pneumocytes from late pregnancy. Premature babies may lack it and develop respiratory distress syndrome.

rush.question: A baby born at 28 weeks is grunting with nasal flaring. Which deficiency is most likely?
rush.why: Preterm lungs produce too little surfactant, causing neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

terms.clue: Narrowing of blood vessels
terms.definition: Narrowing of blood vessels caused by contraction of their smooth muscle.
terms.explanation: It raises vascular resistance and blood pressure, and redirects blood toward vital organs, as in shock or cold.

terms.clue: Stretch sensor that detects blood pressure
terms.definition: A stretch receptor in the carotid sinus and aortic arch that senses changes in blood pressure.
terms.explanation: It drives the baroreflex: a rise in pressure slows the heart and dilates vessels within seconds.

terms.clue: Biological catalyst
terms.definition: A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up reactions by lowering activation energy.
terms.explanation: Enzyme names usually end in -ase, such as lipase and amylase. They are not used up in the reaction.

terms.clue: Six-carbon sugar that fuels most cells
terms.definition: A six-carbon monosaccharide that is the body's main energy source.
terms.explanation: Normal fasting blood glucose is roughly 3.9 to 5.5 mmol/L (70 to 99 mg/dL). The brain depends on it heavily.

terms.clue: Most abundant protein in the body
terms.definition: A triple-helix structural protein found in skin, bone, tendon and blood vessels.
terms.explanation: Vitamin C is needed to make stable collagen, so deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

terms.clue: Splitting glucose into two pyruvate
terms.definition: The pathway in the cytoplasm that breaks one glucose into two pyruvate molecules.
terms.explanation: It gives a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH, and works without oxygen.

terms.clue: Raised ketone bodies from burning fat
terms.definition: A state of raised ketone bodies produced when the body breaks down fat for energy.
terms.explanation: Mild ketosis occurs in fasting. Uncontrolled ketosis with acidosis is diabetic ketoacidosis.

rush.question: Type 1 diabetic: glucose 28 mmol/L, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath. Most likely?
rush.why: Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath with high glucose point to DKA. The deep breathing compensates for metabolic acidosis.

terms.clue: Organelles where most ATP is made
terms.definition: Cell organelles where oxidative phosphorylation produces most of the cell's ATP.
terms.explanation: They have their own DNA, which is inherited from the mother.

terms.clue: Making new glucose from non-sugar sources
terms.definition: Synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, glycerol and amino acids.
terms.explanation: Happens mainly in the liver during fasting, and is stimulated by glucagon and cortisol.

terms.clue: Adding a phosphate group
terms.definition: The addition of a phosphate group to a molecule, often by an enzyme called a kinase.
terms.explanation: It switches many enzymes on or off. Oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria makes most ATP.

terms.clue: Swelling from excess tissue fluid
terms.definition: Swelling caused by excess fluid in the interstitial spaces.
terms.explanation: Causes include heart failure, low albumin, venous obstruction and inflammation. Pitting edema leaves a dent when pressed.

terms.clue: An abnormal mass of tissue
terms.definition: An abnormal growth of tissue, which can be benign or malignant.
terms.explanation: Also called a neoplasm. 'Tumor' is also one of the classic signs of inflammation, meaning swelling.

terms.clue: Uncontrolled cell death from injury
terms.definition: Death of cells or tissue due to injury, such as lost blood supply, toxins or infection.
terms.explanation: Unlike apoptosis, cell contents spill out and trigger inflammation.

terms.clue: Programmed, tidy cell death
terms.definition: Programmed cell death carried out by caspase enzymes without inflammation.
terms.explanation: Normal in development and tissue turnover. Cancers often escape it.

terms.clue: Tissue death from a blocked blood supply
terms.definition: Death of tissue caused by an interruption of its blood supply.
terms.explanation: Myocardial infarction is a heart attack, and cerebral infarction is an ischemic stroke.

terms.clue: Cancer spreading to distant sites
terms.definition: Spread of cancer cells from the primary site to distant parts of the body.
terms.explanation: Spread happens through blood, lymphatics or body cavities. It is the main cause of cancer deaths.

terms.clue: More cells, not bigger cells
terms.definition: An increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ.
terms.explanation: Compare hypertrophy, an increase in cell size. Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a common example.

terms.clue: Fatty plaques hardening the arteries
terms.definition: Build-up of lipid-rich plaques in artery walls, causing narrowing and hardening.
terms.explanation: It underlies most heart attacks, strokes and peripheral arterial disease.

rush.question: Which is a major MODIFIABLE risk factor for atherosclerosis?
rush.why: Smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol and diabetes can be changed. Age, sex and family history cannot.

terms.clue: An inactive 'dummy' treatment
terms.definition: An inactive substance or sham treatment used as a control in trials.
terms.explanation: Patients may still improve because of expectation, which is the placebo effect.

terms.clue: A painkiller
terms.definition: A drug that relieves pain without causing loss of consciousness.
terms.explanation: Examples include paracetamol, NSAIDs and opioids, usually stepped up following the WHO analgesic ladder.

terms.clue: Kills or stops bacteria, not viruses
terms.definition: A drug that kills bacteria or inhibits their growth.
terms.explanation: Antibiotics do not work against viruses. Overuse drives antimicrobial resistance.

terms.clue: Binds a receptor and switches it on
terms.definition: A drug that binds a receptor and activates it.
terms.explanation: Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist that relaxes airway smooth muscle.

terms.clue: A 'water tablet' that increases urine output
terms.definition: A drug that increases urine production by the kidneys.
terms.explanation: Loop diuretics such as furosemide are used in heart failure. Thiazides are used in hypertension.

rush.question: Furosemide commonly causes which electrolyte disturbance?
rush.why: Loop diuretics increase potassium loss in urine, so potassium needs monitoring.

terms.clue: Binds a receptor and blocks it
terms.definition: A drug that binds a receptor without activating it, blocking the action of agonists.
terms.explanation: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that reverses opioid overdose.

rush.question: Pinpoint pupils and a breathing rate of 6/min after heroin use. Which drug?
rush.why: Naloxone competitively blocks opioid receptors and reverses respiratory depression.

terms.clue: Blood thinner that prevents clots
terms.definition: A drug that reduces the blood's ability to clot.
terms.explanation: Examples are warfarin, heparin and DOACs such as apixaban. The main risk is bleeding.

rush.question: Warfarin's effect is monitored with which blood test?
rush.why: The INR (international normalised ratio) measures how long blood takes to clot on warfarin.

terms.clue: Fraction of a dose reaching the circulation
terms.definition: The proportion of a drug dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.
terms.explanation: IV drugs have 100% bioavailability. Oral doses are often reduced by first-pass metabolism in the liver.

terms.clue: Replicates only inside living cells
terms.definition: A tiny infectious agent of nucleic acid in a protein coat that replicates only inside host cells.
terms.explanation: Viruses contain DNA or RNA but not both. Antibiotics do not kill them.

terms.clue: Yeasts and moulds belong here
terms.definition: A eukaryotic organism such as a yeast or mould.
terms.explanation: Candida is a yeast that causes thrush, especially after antibiotics or in immunosuppression.

terms.clue: Single-celled organisms with no nucleus
terms.definition: Single-celled prokaryotic organisms without a membrane-bound nucleus.
terms.explanation: Gram staining sorts them into gram-positive and gram-negative by cell wall structure.

terms.clue: Any organism that causes disease
terms.definition: A microorganism or agent that causes disease.
terms.explanation: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites and prions.

terms.clue: Spiral-shaped bacterium
terms.definition: A spiral-shaped, motile bacterium.
terms.explanation: Examples include Treponema pallidum (syphilis) and Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease).

terms.clue: Gram-negative cell wall toxin behind septic shock
terms.definition: Lipopolysaccharide from the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria.
terms.explanation: Released when bacteria die. It triggers a strong inflammatory response that can cause septic shock.

terms.clue: Destroying all microbes, spores included
terms.definition: A process that destroys all microorganisms, including bacterial spores.
terms.explanation: Autoclaving uses pressurised steam. Disinfection is weaker and may not kill spores.

terms.clue: Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters
terms.definition: A genus of gram-positive cocci that grow in clusters.
terms.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus causes skin infections, abscesses and sepsis. MRSA is a resistant strain.

terms.clue: Molecule the immune system recognises
terms.definition: A substance that is recognised by the immune system and can trigger a response.
terms.explanation: Antibodies and T-cell receptors bind specific parts of antigens called epitopes.

terms.clue: Trains immunity without causing the disease
terms.definition: A preparation that stimulates immunity to a disease without causing the disease.
terms.explanation: It creates memory B and T cells, so later exposure triggers a fast, strong response.

terms.clue: Y-shaped protein made by plasma cells
terms.definition: A Y-shaped immunoglobulin produced by plasma cells that binds a specific antigen.
terms.explanation: There are five classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD. IgM appears first in a new infection.

terms.clue: White cell family of B, T and NK cells
terms.definition: A type of white blood cell that includes B cells, T cells and natural killer cells.
terms.explanation: These cells drive adaptive immunity. HIV depletes CD4 helper T lymphocytes.

terms.clue: 'Big eater' cell derived from monocytes
terms.definition: A large phagocytic cell derived from monocytes that engulfs pathogens and debris.
terms.explanation: It also presents antigens to T cells and releases inflammatory cytokines.

terms.clue: Severe, life-threatening allergic reaction
terms.definition: A severe, rapid, systemic allergic reaction that can cause airway swelling and shock.
terms.explanation: First-line treatment is intramuscular adrenaline. Mast cell degranulation releases histamine.

rush.question: After a bee sting: wheeze, low blood pressure and lip swelling. First-line treatment?
rush.why: IM adrenaline is life-saving in anaphylaxis. Antihistamines are only adjuncts.

terms.clue: Redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function
terms.definition: The protective response of tissue to injury or infection.
terms.explanation: The classic signs are rubor, calor, tumor, dolor and functio laesa.

terms.clue: When the immune system attacks self
terms.definition: An immune response directed against the body's own tissues.
terms.explanation: Examples include type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

terms.clue: Basic unit of heredity
terms.definition: A segment of DNA that codes for a functional product, usually a protein.
terms.explanation: Humans have around 20,000 protein-coding genes.

terms.clue: One version of a gene
terms.definition: One of the alternative forms of a gene at a given position.
terms.explanation: You inherit one allele of each autosomal gene from each parent.

terms.clue: A change in the DNA sequence
terms.definition: A permanent change in the DNA sequence.
terms.explanation: Mutations can be harmless, harmful or occasionally beneficial. Germline mutations can be inherited.

terms.clue: Three copies of one chromosome
terms.definition: The presence of three copies of a chromosome instead of two.
terms.explanation: Trisomy 21 is Down syndrome. Trisomies 18 (Edwards) and 13 (Patau) are more severe.

rush.question: Which factor most increases the risk of Down syndrome?
rush.why: Nondisjunction in the egg becomes more common with maternal age.

terms.clue: Thread of DNA wound around histones
terms.definition: A structure of DNA packaged around histone proteins that carries genes.
terms.explanation: Human cells normally have 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.

terms.clue: Picture of a person's full chromosome set
terms.definition: The number and appearance of an individual's chromosomes, arranged in pairs.
terms.explanation: Down syndrome appears as 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21.

terms.clue: The traits you can observe
terms.definition: The observable characteristics of an individual, from genotype and environment.
terms.explanation: Two people with the same genotype can have different phenotypes because of environment.

terms.clue: Carrying two different alleles
terms.definition: Having two different alleles of a particular gene.
terms.explanation: Heterozygous carriers of recessive conditions such as cystic fibrosis are usually unaffected.

terms.clue: Low hemoglobin
terms.definition: A reduced hemoglobin concentration or red cell mass, lowering oxygen delivery.
terms.explanation: It is classified by red cell size: microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic.

rush.question: Microcytic anaemia in a woman with heavy periods is most often due to?
rush.why: Chronic blood loss depletes iron stores, which causes small, pale red cells.

terms.clue: Cell fragment that plugs bleeding
terms.definition: A small cell fragment from megakaryocytes that forms the first plug in clotting.
terms.explanation: The normal count is about 150 to 400 x 10^9/L. Aspirin makes platelets less sticky.

terms.clue: Cancer of the blood-forming cells
terms.definition: A cancer of blood-forming tissue that produces abnormal white blood cells.
terms.explanation: It can be acute or chronic, and lymphoid or myeloid. ALL is the commonest childhood cancer.

terms.clue: Iron-containing oxygen carrier in red cells
terms.definition: The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
terms.explanation: Adult hemoglobin has two alpha and two beta chains, each with a heme group.

terms.clue: Formal name for a red blood cell
terms.definition: A red blood cell.
terms.explanation: It has no nucleus, a biconcave shape and a lifespan of about 120 days.

terms.clue: The process of blood clotting
terms.definition: The process by which blood forms a clot.
terms.explanation: A cascade of clotting factors ends with thrombin turning fibrinogen into fibrin.

terms.clue: Inherited X-linked bleeding disorder
terms.definition: An inherited deficiency of a clotting factor that causes prolonged bleeding.
terms.explanation: Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency and B is factor IX. Both are X-linked, so mostly males are affected.

terms.clue: A low platelet count
terms.definition: A platelet count below the normal range, usually under 150 x 10^9/L.
terms.explanation: It raises the risk of bruising, petechiae and bleeding. Causes include ITP, drugs and marrow failure.

terms.clue: A nerve cell
terms.definition: A cell that transmits electrical and chemical signals in the nervous system.
terms.explanation: Its parts are the dendrites (input), the cell body, and the axon (output).

terms.clue: Sudden brain injury from a blocked or burst vessel
terms.definition: Sudden loss of brain function due to interrupted blood supply (ischemic) or bleeding (hemorrhagic).
terms.explanation: Recognise it with FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time. Treatment depends on time since onset.

rush.question: Facial droop and arm weakness began 40 minutes ago. Key first investigation?
rush.why: CT excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis can be considered.

terms.clue: Fatty sheath insulating axons
terms.definition: A fatty insulating layer around many axons that speeds nerve conduction.
terms.explanation: Oligodendrocytes make it in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS. Multiple sclerosis destroys CNS myelin.

terms.clue: Burst of abnormal electrical brain activity
terms.definition: A transient episode of abnormal, excessive, synchronised neuronal activity.
terms.explanation: A seizure lasting over 5 minutes needs emergency treatment, often a benzodiazepine.

terms.clue: Progressive decline in memory and thinking
terms.definition: A progressive decline in cognitive function severe enough to affect daily life.
terms.explanation: Alzheimer disease is the commonest cause, followed by vascular dementia.

terms.clue: Inflammation of the brain's coverings
terms.definition: Inflammation of the meninges, the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.
terms.explanation: Classic features are fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. Bacterial meningitis is an emergency.

rush.question: Suspected meningococcal disease with a non-blanching rash, outside hospital. Best action?
rush.why: Early antibiotics save lives in meningococcal sepsis. Do not delay to investigate.

terms.clue: Pins and needles
terms.definition: An abnormal sensation such as tingling or prickling without an external stimulus.
terms.explanation: Common causes include nerve compression (carpal tunnel), B12 deficiency and diabetic neuropathy.

terms.clue: Chemical messenger crossing the synapse
terms.definition: A chemical released by neurons to signal across a synapse.
terms.explanation: Examples include acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, GABA and glutamate.

terms.clue: Rhythmic arterial throb felt at the wrist
terms.definition: The rhythmic expansion of an artery with each heartbeat.
terms.explanation: A normal adult resting rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Check the rate, rhythm and volume.

terms.clue: Chest pain from heart muscle ischemia
terms.definition: Chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle.
terms.explanation: Stable angina comes on with exertion and settles with rest or GTN spray.

terms.clue: Heart rate above 100
terms.definition: A resting heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
terms.explanation: Causes include fever, pain, dehydration, anaemia, sepsis and arrhythmias.

terms.clue: Heart rate below 60
terms.definition: A resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute.
terms.explanation: Can be normal in athletes. Pathological causes include heart block, beta-blockers and hypothyroidism.

terms.clue: Persistently raised blood pressure
terms.definition: Persistently high blood pressure, typically 140/90 mmHg or above in clinic.
terms.explanation: Often silent, it damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over time.

rush.question: BP is 180/120 mmHg. What must you assess for urgently?
rush.why: Check for organ damage such as chest pain, neurological signs, retinal changes and kidney injury to identify a hypertensive emergency.

terms.clue: An irregular or abnormal heart rhythm
terms.definition: Any abnormality of the heart's rate or rhythm.
terms.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is the commonest sustained arrhythmia and raises stroke risk.

terms.clue: The muscular middle layer of the heart wall
terms.definition: The muscular layer of the heart wall.
terms.explanation: It sits between the endocardium and the epicardium. A heart attack is myocardial infarction.

terms.clue: Recording of the heart's electrical activity
terms.definition: A recording of the heart's electrical activity, usually from 12 leads.
terms.explanation: It is used to detect ischemia, infarction, arrhythmias and electrolyte effects.

rush.question: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF suggests which territory of MI?
rush.why: II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery.

terms.clue: Reversible airway narrowing with wheeze
terms.definition: A chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible bronchoconstriction.
terms.explanation: Symptoms are wheeze, cough and breathlessness, often at night. Treated with inhaled steroids and bronchodilators.

terms.clue: Tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens
terms.definition: The tiny air sacs at the end of the airways where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
terms.explanation: Hundreds of millions of them give a gas-exchange surface of around 70 square metres.

terms.clue: Not enough oxygen reaching the tissues
terms.definition: Inadequate oxygen supply at the tissue level.
terms.explanation: Hypoxaemia means low oxygen in the blood, which is one cause of hypoxia.

terms.clue: Infection filling the lung tissue
terms.definition: Infection and inflammation of the lung tissue, with alveoli filling with fluid or pus.
terms.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest bacterial cause. Severity can be scored with CURB-65.

rush.question: Which finding scores a point in CURB-65?
rush.why: CURB-65 is Confusion, Urea over 7, Respiratory rate of 30 or more, low Blood pressure and age 65 or over.

terms.clue: Inflamed bronchi with a productive cough
terms.definition: Inflammation of the bronchi, causing cough with sputum.
terms.explanation: Acute bronchitis is usually viral. Chronic bronchitis is a productive cough for 3 months in 2 consecutive years and is part of COPD.

terms.clue: Destroyed alveolar walls, usually from smoking
terms.definition: Permanent enlargement of air spaces with destruction of alveolar walls.
terms.explanation: Part of COPD, mostly caused by smoking. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a rarer cause in young people.

terms.clue: Breathing test measuring FEV1 and FVC
terms.definition: A lung function test that measures how much air and how fast it can be exhaled.
terms.explanation: An FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 indicates airflow obstruction, as in COPD or asthma.

terms.clue: Air in the pleural space collapsing a lung
terms.definition: Air in the pleural space, causing partial or complete lung collapse.
terms.explanation: A tension pneumothorax is an emergency: trachea deviated away, hypotension and absent breath sounds on the affected side.

rush.question: Trauma: absent breath sounds on one side, trachea deviated away, falling BP. Immediate action?
rush.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Decompress immediately without waiting for imaging.

terms.clue: Largest solid internal organ
terms.definition: The large organ in the right upper abdomen that metabolises nutrients and drugs and makes bile and proteins.
terms.explanation: It makes albumin and clotting factors, so liver failure causes edema and bleeding.

terms.clue: A break in the lining of the gut or skin
terms.definition: A break in the surface lining of skin or a mucous membrane.
terms.explanation: Peptic ulcers are mostly caused by Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs.

terms.clue: Inflammation of the liver
terms.definition: Inflammation of the liver.
terms.explanation: Causes include viruses (hepatitis A to E), alcohol, drugs and autoimmune disease.

terms.clue: Yellow skin and eyes
terms.definition: Yellowing of the skin and sclerae caused by raised bilirubin.
terms.explanation: It can be pre-hepatic (hemolysis), hepatic or post-hepatic (obstruction). Pale stools and dark urine suggest obstruction.

terms.clue: End-stage scarring of the liver
terms.definition: Irreversible scarring of the liver with regenerative nodules.
terms.explanation: Common causes are alcohol, hepatitis B and C, and fatty liver disease. Complications include ascites and varices.

terms.clue: Pain that starts at the navel and moves right
terms.definition: Inflammation of the appendix.
terms.explanation: Pain typically starts around the umbilicus and moves to the right iliac fossa (McBurney's point).

rush.question: Pain began around the umbilicus and moved to the right iliac fossa, with fever. Most likely?
rush.why: Migrating periumbilical pain to the RIF is the classic appendicitis story.

terms.clue: Epigastric pain to the back with high lipase
terms.definition: Inflammation of the pancreas.
terms.explanation: Gallstones and alcohol are the main causes. Serum lipase or amylase is markedly raised.

terms.clue: Inflamed gallbladder with a positive Murphy's sign
terms.definition: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by a gallstone blocking the cystic duct.
terms.explanation: Causes right upper quadrant pain, fever and a positive Murphy's sign.

terms.clue: Beta-cell hormone that lowers blood glucose
terms.definition: A hormone from pancreatic beta cells that lowers blood glucose.
terms.explanation: It moves glucose into cells and promotes storage. Absent in type 1 diabetes.

terms.clue: Butterfly-shaped gland in the neck
terms.definition: An endocrine gland in the neck that produces T3 and T4.
terms.explanation: Thyroid hormones set metabolic rate. Its function is checked with TSH and free T4.

terms.clue: Main stress hormone from the adrenal cortex
terms.definition: A glucocorticoid hormone from the adrenal cortex involved in the stress response.
terms.explanation: Excess causes Cushing syndrome and deficiency causes Addison disease.

terms.clue: Chronic high blood sugar
terms.definition: Diabetes mellitus: chronic hyperglycemia from insulin deficiency, insulin resistance, or both.
terms.explanation: Symptoms are thirst, polyuria and weight loss. Long-term effects damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves and vessels.

rush.question: Which HbA1c level supports a diagnosis of diabetes?
rush.why: An HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above is diagnostic of diabetes.

terms.clue: Alpha-cell hormone that raises blood glucose
terms.definition: A hormone from pancreatic alpha cells that raises blood glucose.
terms.explanation: It stimulates glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis in the liver. IM glucagon treats severe hypoglycaemia.

terms.clue: Fight-or-flight hormone from the adrenal medulla
terms.definition: Epinephrine: a hormone and neurotransmitter from the adrenal medulla.
terms.explanation: It raises heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, and dilates airways. It is first-line in anaphylaxis.

terms.clue: The 'master gland' in the sella turcica
terms.definition: A pea-sized endocrine gland at the base of the brain that controls other glands.
terms.explanation: It releases TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, growth hormone and prolactin. A tumour can compress the optic chiasm.

terms.clue: Underactive thyroid
terms.definition: Deficient thyroid hormone production.
terms.explanation: Causes fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation. Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause where iodine is sufficient.

rush.question: Raised TSH with low free T4 indicates?
rush.why: A failing thyroid makes little T4, so the pituitary raises TSH to compensate.
